stories.headline: Trump swaps Susie Wiles for Stephen Miller as chief of staff
stories.summary: Three days after Republicans lost both chambers, President Trump announced on Truth Social that Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, architect of the administration's hard-line immigration agenda, will become White House chief of staff on Monday, Nov. 9. Susie Wiles, his longest-serving chief of staff and the first woman in the job, resigned Thursday night and moves to Trump's political operation. Axios reported Trump blamed her for the losses, even though she had privately opposed the Iran war and questioned Miller's immigration tactics. A Trump adviser called Miller "a wartime adviser" for the coming fight with Democratic investigations.
stories.side_a: Critics say Trump is punishing the aide who warned him and promoting the man whose policies voters just rejected. To them it reads as doubling down on the immigration raids and war that drove the rout, and as a signal that the White House is preparing for confrontation with Congress rather than compromise.
stories.side_b: Supporters say a president is entitled to the staff he trusts, that Miller knows the levers of the executive branch better than anyone, and that a divided government facing subpoenas and hearings needs a fighter rather than a manager. They argue the base wants the agenda carried out, not softened.
stories.question_underneath: When a leader is rebuked, should he change course or change the people around him? Who bears responsibility for a defeat: the advisor or the one advised?
stories.thinkers_note: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 22-23: a prince is judged by the counselors he keeps, and flatterers are the court's great danger. The biblical story of Rehoboam (1 Kings 12): rejecting the elders' counsel for the young hard-liners' and losing the kingdom. The ancient Greek pharmakos ritual and René Girard's scapegoat theory: expelling one person to purge a collective failure.

stories.headline: Hegseth defiant as a Republican readies impeachment articles
stories.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posted a video Thursday calling Rep. Thomas Massie's renewed impeachment push "sham articles" and "the politics of personal destruction." Massie, who lost his GOP primary after crossing Trump, says he will reintroduce the articles when the House returns Monday unless Hegseth resigns, warning that Democrats in the new Congress will bring "hearings & trials." Democracy Now reported Hegseth also called for at least $350 billion more in military funding. Trump says Hegseth has done "a fantastic job," though NBC reported he has privately asked allies about possible successors. Only two Cabinet officials have ever been impeached.
stories.side_a: Supporters of impeachment say the Iran war was waged without congressional authorization, cost American lives and money, and that Congress must enforce accountability on the man running it. For Massie and some Republicans, it is about constitutional war powers, not party.
stories.side_b: Hegseth's defenders say impeachment is meant for high crimes, not policy disagreements; that a lame-duck vote driven by an outgoing member is pure politics; and that removing a war secretary mid-conflict signals weakness to Iran. They note the Senate has never convicted a Cabinet member.
stories.question_underneath: Is impeachment a remedy for crimes only, or also for grave misjudgment? How should a republic hold the conduct of war accountable without paralyzing it?
stories.thinkers_note: Federalist No. 65 (Hamilton): impeachment covers "the abuse or violation of some public trust," political by nature. Locke's Second Treatise on the federative power (war and peace) and its tension with legislative supremacy. Cicero's maxim "inter arma enim silent leges" (in war the laws fall silent), and the republican worry it describes.

stories.headline: Newly elected Democratic senators turn on Chuck Schumer
stories.summary: A growing list of incoming Democratic senators, including Adam Hamilton (Kansas), Abdul El-Sayed (Michigan), James Talarico (Texas), Juliana Stratton (Illinois), Peggy Flanagan (Minnesota), Troy Jackson (Maine), Chris Pappas (New Hampshire), and South Carolina's Annie Andrews (who called for "generational change"), say they won't back Schumer, 75, as majority leader. The Guardian reports Schumer likely still has the caucus votes and no challenger has formally emerged; he says, "I'll be re-elected as majority leader." Mississippi and Alaska Senate races were still uncalled Friday.
stories.side_a: The newcomers say voters asked for change, that the party's aging leadership presided over years of frustration, and that a wave election built on new faces should produce new leadership. Many ran explicitly as independent from the Washington establishment and want to keep that promise.
stories.side_b: Schumer's allies say experience matters most when facing a hostile White House, that he just led the party to a sweeping majority, and that a leadership fight now would squander the momentum. Some note that newcomers rarely understand Senate procedure on day one.
stories.question_underneath: What do generations owe each other in political leadership? When does experience become entrenchment?
stories.thinkers_note: Plato's Republic on the education and succession of guardians: how a regime renews its leadership without upheaval. Ecclesiastes 3: "a time to plant, and a time to uproot"; the wisdom of knowing when one's season has ended. Washington's farewell and the norm of voluntary retirement as a republican virtue.

stories.headline: Judge halts Trump's 250-foot arch hours after it won approval
stories.summary: Less than two hours after the National Capital Planning Commission, after a roughly nine-hour hearing dominated by opponents, approved President Trump's triumphal arch at Memorial Circle by 8-4, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day order barring any construction. The arch, at 250 feet for the nation's 250th anniversary, would stand between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. In a 33-page opinion, Chutkan found D.C. and Virginia would likely suffer real harm and called the administration's reliance on a century-old bridge statute, and its late national-security rationale, a stretch.
stories.side_a: Opponents, including veterans and local governments, say a giant arch at the gateway to Arlington would turn sacred ground into a personal monument, ignore the Commemorative Works Act's requirement of national consensus, and snarl traffic for years. They see it as a president building in stone what he could not win at the ballot box.
stories.side_b: Supporters say great nations build monuments to their founding and their victories, that Washington's classical landscape was itself once controversial, and that the arch honors America's 250th birthday, not one man. They see the ruling as judicial obstruction of a lawful federal project.
stories.question_underneath: Who has the right to shape a nation's sacred spaces? What makes a monument a shared memory rather than one ruler's signature?
stories.thinkers_note: Shelley's "Ozymandias": monuments outlast the power that raised them and can mock it. Pericles' building program in Athens: civic glory or personal vanity, debated in Plutarch's Life of Pericles. Arendt on the "common world": public things that outlast us and must belong to everyone.

stories.headline: Italy plans a state museum for Mussolini's favorite painter
stories.summary: Italy's culture ministry under Giorgia Meloni plans to open a Mario Sironi museum in Rome in 2027, with about 30 newly acquired works and 90 loans, housed in a 1928 fascist-era veterans' building that holds Sironi frescoes including one of Mussolini on horseback. Culture minister Alessandro Giuli called it the achievement he is proudest of. The Art Newspaper notes press materials do not mention fascism; Sironi joined the movement in 1919 and drew more than 1,700 cartoons for Mussolini's newspaper. Historians Tomaso Montanari and Fabio Benzi warn the museum must not become an endorsement of fascism or an authoritarian aesthetic.
stories.side_a: Critics say a right-wing government with neo-fascist roots is quietly rehabilitating fascist aesthetics, and that a national museum silent about Sironi's politics in a fascist monument is not neutral. Italy's republic was founded on anti-fascism, Montanari says, and its museums should say so.
stories.side_b: Defenders say Sironi is a major Modernist whose art deserves serious study, that great art made under bad regimes is still great art, and that ignoring him impoverishes Italian art history. Montanari himself doesn't oppose the museum; the question is framing, not existence.
stories.question_underneath: Can we honor the art without honoring the cause? What does a nation owe its past: forgetting, condemnation, or honest remembrance?
stories.thinkers_note: Walter Benjamin's warning about the "aestheticization of politics" under fascism. Plato's Republic, Book III and X: the city's concern with what art teaches its citizens. Nietzsche's "On the Use and Abuse of History for Life": monumental, antiquarian and critical history, each with its dangers.

stories.headline: French court orders a Nazi-looted Pissarro returned, even after a Sotheby's sale
stories.summary: A Paris court ruled Nov. 5 that Camille Pissarro's 1902 view of Dieppe's harbor, seized from Jewish banker Salomon Flavian in Paris in 1941, must be returned to his heirs, voiding every sale since, including Sotheby's London sale in June 2024 for 1.2 million pounds. Sotheby's has two months to identify the buyer or pay 1,000 euros a day. The sale relied on a settlement signed by only two of the heirs through Mondex, a looted-art recovery firm; Mondex plans to appeal and Sotheby's says enforcing the ruling in the UK requires its own procedure.
stories.side_a: The family's lawyer calls it a vital ruling: theft does not become ownership through time or resale, and every later buyer inherits the original wrong. Restitution is a debt still owed to victims of the Holocaust and their families.
stories.side_b: Mondex and the auction world argue the painting's history is genuinely contested, that good-faith buyers and settlements need finality, and that a French court reaching into a London sale threatens legal certainty. Sotheby's stresses client confidentiality and notes all claims against it were dismissed.
stories.question_underneath: Does a wrong ever expire? How long does justice owe a debt to the dispossessed, and who pays it when the thief is long gone?
stories.thinkers_note: Roman law's maxim "nemo dat quod non habet": no one can give what they do not own. Locke on property and theft: unjust acquisition cannot ground a just title. Burke's society as a partnership between the dead, the living, and the unborn, with debts that pass between generations.

stories.headline: Newsom clears California's death row; Catholic abolitionists cheer, victims' advocates protest
stories.summary: Gov. Gavin Newsom moved Thursday to commute the death sentences of all 548 people on California's death row to life without parole, the largest act of mass clemency in U.S. history according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Nearly 400 cases need approval from four of seven state Supreme Court justices. "These offenders will die in prison but not by our hand," he wrote. The Catholic Mobilizing Network welcomed the decision. Victims' groups condemned it; the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation's Anne Marie Schubert vowed a court challenge, and Polly Klaas's father said it "upsets me terribly," while her sister said execution doesn't bring healing.
stories.side_a: Abolitionists, including Catholic advocates following the Church's teaching that the death penalty is inadmissible, say the state should not kill, that the system is marked by racial disparity and error, and that life without parole protects the public while leaving room for repentance.
stories.side_b: Victims' advocates say one governor overrode juries, judges and voters, who in 2016 chose to speed executions rather than abolish them. Many religious defenders of capital punishment cite Genesis 9:6 and Romans 13, arguing that justice for the gravest murders requires the gravest penalty.
stories.question_underneath: Is mercy an act of justice or a departure from it? Does the state hold the sword on God's behalf, or should it lay it down?
stories.thinkers_note: Genesis 9:6 ("whoever sheds man's blood") and Romans 13:4 (the ruler "does not bear the sword in vain") versus John 8:7 ("let him who is without sin cast the first stone"). Kant's retributivism (justice demands proportional punishment) versus Beccaria's On Crimes and Punishments. The 2018 revision of the Catholic Catechism, para. 2267, declaring the death penalty "inadmissible."

stories.headline: Pope Leo, three weeks after cancer surgery, calls for universal health care in Uruguay
stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV began a 12-day, three-country tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Friday, his first major trip since surgery to remove part of a lung. In Montevideo, beside left-wing President Yamandu Orsi, he called accessible health care "a duty that confronts every society," citing his own recent illness. In a country that legalized abortion in 2012 and euthanasia this year, he urged care from the womb to "the natural end" of life, addressed Uruguay's high suicide rate, and said a secular state must not confine religion to private life.
stories.side_a: Admirers see a consistent ethic of life: a pope who just needed care himself demanding it for the poor, while also defending the unborn, the suicidal, and the dying. He offers a vision that crosses partisan lines.
stories.side_b: Secular Uruguayans and liberal critics say a foreign religious leader shouldn't lecture a democracy about laws its people chose, like abortion and euthanasia. Some conservatives, meanwhile, bristle at a pope endorsing government-guaranteed health care as a moral duty rather than leaving it to prudential judgment.
stories.question_underneath: What does a secular state owe to religious voices, and what do religious voices owe to a secular state? Is care for the sick a matter of charity, justice, or both?
stories.thinkers_note: The parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10) and Matthew 25's "I was sick and you visited me." Jacques Maritain on the secular state that still draws on Christian moral sources. John Rawls's "public reason" versus the view that religious arguments belong fully in public debate.

stories.headline: Hebron's shared holy site closed to Muslims as thousands of Jews gather for Shabbat Chayei Sarah
stories.summary: Israeli forces closed Hebron's Ibrahimi Mosque, which Jews call the Cave of the Patriarchs and both faiths revere as Abraham's burial place, to Palestinian worshippers from Friday afternoon until Saturday night, Al Jazeera reported, as Jewish visitors arrived for the Torah portion about Sarah's burial there. Israeli forces told The Jerusalem Post they expected about 20,000 visitors; Chabad put the figure at 45,000. Palestinians report tightened checkpoints in the Old City, following a 10-day Israeli operation in Hebron and a June move by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich to take over planning powers at the site.
stories.side_a: Palestinians and their supporters say barring Muslims from a working mosque, suspending the call to prayer, and confining residents to their homes for a settler gathering is collective punishment and a step toward taking the site for exclusive Jewish use.
stories.side_b: Israelis and Jewish visitors say Hebron is one of Judaism's four holy cities, that Jews were barred from the cave for centuries, and that the arrangement gives each community exclusive days a few times a year. They say the security measures are needed to protect large crowds in a volatile city.
stories.question_underneath: Can two peoples share a sacred place they both claim through the same father? What does justice look like when holiness itself is contested?
stories.thinkers_note: Genesis 23 and 25: Abraham buys the cave to bury Sarah, and Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham together. Augustine's two cities, and the danger of confusing earthly possession with divine promise. Mircea Eliade on sacred space: why holy ground is felt as non-negotiable, and so hard to divide.
